summary.en: Rooted in blues, the Rolling Stones appear and begin early songwriting.
summary.zh: 根植于布鲁斯的The Rolling Stones出现，并开始初期创作。

body.zh:
上节课我们讲到上世纪60年代初伦敦的布鲁斯复兴者以及布鲁斯俱乐部场景，Keith Richards、Mick Jagger和Brian Jones等人经常出没于此，他们都是很棒的布鲁斯音乐爱好者，The Rolling Stones就是在那种环境下诞生的。他们是一群年轻伙伴，努力模仿着追随的前辈们。

乐队最初的领头人是Brian Jones，我们都以为The Rolling Stones是由Mick和Keith领导的，其实Brian Jones才是乐队领袖，他是一个真正的布鲁斯狂热爱好者。所以当Keith Richards和Mick Jagger想翻唱Chuck Berry和Buddy Holly的曲子时，Brain Jones就不太愿意了，因为他太坚持布鲁斯了，连这样的翻唱他都觉得是向商业主义出卖自己，这跟60年代美国格林威治村的民谣狂热者差不多。

当时的布鲁斯狂热者，都不希望别人认为自己是为了名利才演奏布鲁斯的。如果你是彼时英国的布鲁斯狂热者，你真的是因为音乐本身才从事这个行业。有个故事是关于Eric Clapton的，他在录制The YardBirds的第一首单曲时退出了乐队，因为乐队不能真正参与到唱片当中，Eric把那些流行乐当作垃圾，然后说算了吧，我要住到柴房里去，成为一个更好的布鲁斯玩家。现在所说的就是他这种态度，置名利于脑后。如果名利对你来说很重要，那么你对布鲁斯就是不忠诚的。Brian Jones就是这种人，乐队名The Rolling Stones也是从布鲁斯传统中吸取而来的，之后就在Crawdaddy俱乐部定期演出。这家俱乐部就在伦敦市中心火车站附近，它的经营者是Giorgio Gomelsky。Giorgio Gomelsky认为，不管从哪个角度看，他都是The Rolling Stones的经纪人，他没有真正跟乐队签合约，但我们都能理解那种情况。乐队在他的俱乐部定期演出，他为乐队宣传，这就是当时的情况。

但后来又杀出了一位Andrew Loog Oldham，他原来是为Brian Epstein工作的，这时出任了The Rolling Stones的经纪人，然后乐队就抛弃了老伙计Giorgio Gomelsky。结果在The Rolling Stones大获成功之后，Giorgio又找了一个叫做The Yardbirds的乐队在自己的俱乐部演出，这次，他肯定签好了合约。

The Rolling Stones在Crawdaddy俱乐部演出的这个时间，你可能回想起我曾经提到过Dick Rowe。他当时在Decca唱片公司，1962年1月他为The Beatles安排了一场试音，然后拒绝了他们。后来Brian Epstein拿着这张试音磁带满伦敦推销，也没人想要，直到最后Parlophone唱片公司的George Martin请The Beatles参加了试音，并最终签下了他们。Dick Rowe曾作为Decca的代表在才艺秀之类的活动里担任嘉宾评委，George Harrison在The Beatles一炮而红之后也担任过这个活动的嘉宾评委。有个广为流传不知是真是假的故事，我觉得George Harrison应该比较讲喜欢它。故事是说，当时George正和Dick Rowe聊天，Dick就向George说起自己错失了The Beatles有多遗憾，George也无法想象这给他带来了多大麻烦，他还因此获得了“错失The Beatles的人”这样的名声。Dick还说，你们乐队获得的巨大成功让我看起来像个傻瓜，你有没有比较看好的歌手或者乐队可以介绍给我？或者前景可能不错的，我可以把他们签下来。George Harrison就跟他说，你可以试试The Rolling Stones，他们就在伦敦火车站隔壁Crawdaddy俱乐部演出。根据George很爱讲的那个版本，当时他说完之后就转过身去看别人了，等他转回头来，看到Dick Rowe的椅子还在转，人已经跑没影了。后来事实证明Dick Rowe确实去Crawdaddy俱乐部见了The Rolling Stones，也确实签下了他们，这场交易中基本没Giorgio Gomelsky什么事，都是Andrew Loog Oldham促成的。

有趣的是，因为The Beatles和Phil Spector有些交情，所以Andrew Loog Oldham从Phil Spector那得到一点建议，他对The Rolling Stones说，要记得永远拥有自己的录音母带，只授权给唱片公司使用，于是The Rolling Stones就这么做了。当时的英国厂牌没觉得这有什么特别的，从来没有别的艺术家这么干过。通常过不了几年，大多数流行乐都已经不在榜单上了，那时谁还在乎母带是谁的呢？不过对于The Rolling Stones来说，这样做让他们获得了意外的好运。因为掌握了母带，在接下来的几十年里，他们带着这些作品换了一个又一个厂牌。

一开始The Rolling Stones并没有像The Beatles那样立刻在美国获得巨大成功，他们最初的几张唱片都是翻唱作品，Keith和Mick还没开始创作歌曲，他们的翻唱作品分为摇滚和R&B，一些重要又有趣的翻唱版本只在英国上榜了，在美国没有。1963年，他们翻唱的Chuck Berry的歌曲《Come On》，登上了英国榜单的第21名。1964年翻唱的Buddy Holly的作品《Not Fade Away》 名列榜单第三。

他们甚至还演唱了Lennon和McCartney写的歌，我之前说过，他们俩（John Lennon和Paul McCartney）原来很想成为一个歌曲创作团队，一旦他们获得成功，就开始把自己的作品卖给其他音乐人。他们卖了一首歌给The Rolling Stones，这首歌是《I Wanna Be Your Man》，它在1963年获得了英国榜第12名。如果你有机会分别听一下The Rolling Stones和The Beatles演唱的 《I Wanna Be Your Man》，可以好好研究一下这两个乐队的差别。The Rolling Stones的版本偏向布鲁斯风格，而The Beatles的版本则比较有Motown或者Atlantic唱片的感觉，偏向人声，更加精致。

不过很快Jagger和Richards就开始自己写歌了，他们俩写的第一首重要歌曲是1965年的《The Last Time》，获得英国榜单第一和美国榜单第九，当然 1965年的《I Can't Get No Satisfaction》也是他俩写的。他们甚至还卖了一首作品给Marianne Faithfull，她在60年代有段时间曾是Mick Jagger的女朋友，这首歌是《As Tears Go By》，它在1964年大获成功，获得了英国榜单第九。你可能听过The Rolling Stones的版本，但它一开始是由Marianne Faithfull演唱且曾风行一时。

以上我们大致了解了The Rolling Stones在英国的发展状况，下节课我们来了解一下他们在美国的成功，以及是如何做到的。
body.en:
Last lecture we covered early-1960s London blues revivalists and the club scene where Keith Richards, Mick Jagger, Brian Jones and others hung out—serious blues fans. The Rolling Stones were born in that world: young mates trying to imitate the elders they followed.

The band’s first leader was Brian Jones. We tend to think Mick and Keith led the Stones, but Brian was the leader—a true blues fanatic. So when Keith and Mick wanted to cover Chuck Berry and Buddy Holly, Brian resisted; he was so blues-purist that even those covers felt like selling out to commercialism—much like Greenwich Village folk purists in 1960s America.

Blues fanatics then did not want to be seen as playing blues for fame or money. If you were a British blues fanatic at that time, you were in it for the music itself. There is a story about Eric Clapton: he quit the Yardbirds while recording their first single because the band could not really own the record; Eric treated that pop as trash and said forget it—he would live in a woodshed and become a better blues player. That is the attitude: put fame aside. If fame mattered to you, you were disloyal to the blues. Brian Jones was that kind of person. The name Rolling Stones also came from blues tradition. They then played regularly at the Crawdaddy Club near a central London station, run by Giorgio Gomelsky. Giorgio thought of himself as the Stones’ manager from every angle; he had no signed contract, but we understand the situation: regular club gigs, he promoted them—that was how it was.

Then Andrew Loog Oldham appeared—formerly working for Brian Epstein—and became the Stones’ manager; the band dropped old friend Giorgio Gomelsky. After the Stones succeeded, Giorgio put another band, the Yardbirds, into his club—and this time he made sure of a contract.

Around the time the Stones played Crawdaddy, you may recall Dick Rowe. He was at Decca; in January 1962 he auditioned the Beatles and turned them down. Brian Epstein hawked that demo around London with no takers until Parlophone’s George Martin auditioned and signed them. Dick Rowe had sat as a guest judge on talent-show–type events; after the Beatles hit, George Harrison also guest-judged one. There is a widely told story—true or not—I think George rather liked it. George was chatting with Dick; Dick said how sorry he was to have missed the Beatles, and George could hardly imagine the trouble that had caused him—he had the reputation as “the man who missed the Beatles.” Dick said the Beatles’ huge success made him look a fool—did George know any promising singer or band he might sign? George told him to try the Rolling Stones, playing at the Crawdaddy next to the London station. In the version George loves to tell, he turned to look at someone else; when he looked back, Dick’s chair was still spinning and Dick was gone. In fact Dick did go to the Crawdaddy, did see the Stones, and did sign them—Giorgio Gomelsky was largely out of that deal; Andrew Loog Oldham made it happen.

Interestingly, because the Beatles had some connection with Phil Spector, Andrew Loog Oldham got a tip from Spector and told the Stones always to own their masters and only license use to the label—and they did. British labels then did not think it special; no other artist had done it. Usually within a few years most pop was off the charts—who cared who owned the masters? For the Stones it proved lucky: holding the masters, over the following decades they moved those recordings from label to label.

At first the Stones did not score huge U.S. success like the Beatles. Early records were covers; Keith and Mick had not started writing yet. Covers were rock and R&B; some important, interesting covers charted only in Britain, not America. In 1963 their cover of Chuck Berry’s “Come On” reached No. 21 in Britain. In 1964 Buddy Holly’s “Not Fade Away” hit No. 3.

They even sang a Lennon–McCartney song. As I said, John and Paul had wanted to be a songwriting team; once successful they began selling songs to other artists. They sold the Stones “I Wanna Be Your Man,” which reached No. 12 in Britain in 1963. If you can hear both the Stones’ and Beatles’ versions, study the difference: the Stones lean blues; the Beatles sound more Motown or Atlantic—more vocal, more polished.

Soon Jagger and Richards began writing. Their first important song was 1965’s “The Last Time”—No. 1 Britain, No. 9 U.S.—and of course 1965’s “(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction” is theirs too. They even sold a song to Marianne Faithfull, Mick’s girlfriend for a stretch in the 1960s—“As Tears Go By,” a 1964 success at No. 9 in Britain. You may know the Stones’ version, but it first hit with Marianne Faithfull.

That roughly covers the Stones in Britain; next lecture: their U.S. success and how they got it.
